questions.question:
Consider a network that uses Ethernet and IPv4. Assume that IPv4 headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of 1500 bytes in its data field. A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is 7488 bytes.
Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including IPv4 header?
questions.explanation:
Ethernet frame data field max [latex]=1500[/latex] bytes; IPv4 header [latex]=20[/latex] bytes (no options), so max IP data per fragment [latex]=1500-20=1480[/latex] bytes — conveniently already a multiple of [latex]8[/latex], so no further rounding needed.

The UDP segment (header [latex]8[/latex] bytes [latex]+[/latex] payload [latex]7488[/latex] bytes [latex]=7496[/latex] bytes) becomes the IP datagram's data, which must be fragmented:
[latex]7496\div1480=5.06\ldots[/latex], so [latex]5[/latex] full fragments of [latex]1480[/latex] bytes ([latex]7400[/latex] bytes) plus a final fragment of [latex]7496-7400=96[/latex] bytes of data.

Total fragments [latex]=5+1=6[/latex]. Last fragment's total size (including its own [latex]20[/latex]-byte IP header) [latex]=96+20=116[/latex] bytes.

Answer: 6 fragments, 116 bytes

questions.question: Which of the following statements is/are true with respect to the interaction of a web browser with a web server using HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex]?

options.A: HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple objects of the same webpage over the same TCP connection, if the objects are stored in the same server
options.B: HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple objects of the same webpage over the same TCP connection, even if they are stored in different servers
options.C: HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates sending a request for downloading one object without waiting for a previously requested object to be downloaded completely
options.D: HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex] facilitates downloading multiple webpages on the same server to be downloaded over a single TCP connection

questions.explanation:
HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections and pipelining over a single TCP connection:

- True: Multiple objects of the same webpage, if hosted on the same server, can be fetched over one persistent TCP connection — this is exactly the point of persistent connections.
- False: A single TCP connection is between one client and one specific server; objects stored on a different server require a separate TCP connection to that server. So this statement is false.
- True: HTTP/1.1 supports pipelining — a client can send a new request before the response to a previous request has been fully received, over the same connection.
- True: Since the TCP connection persists (is not closed after one request/response), multiple different webpages/resources from the same server can be downloaded over that same single connection, one after another.

Answer: Statements 1, 3, and 4 are true (same-server multi-object download, pipelining, multiple pages over one connection); statement about different servers over the same connection is false.

questions.question: Consider the 3-way handshaking protocol for TCP connection establishment. Let the three packets exchanged during the connection establishment be denoted as P1, P2, and P3, in order. Which of the following option(s) is/are TRUE with respect to TCP header flags that are set in the packets?
questions.explanation:
TCP's 3-way handshake, packet by packet:

- P1 (client → server): the client initiates with SYN=1 (and ACK=0, since there's nothing to acknowledge yet).
- P2 (server → client): the server both acknowledges the client's SYN and sends its own SYN, so SYN=1, ACK=1 simultaneously (this combined SYN-ACK packet is the hallmark of TCP's handshake).
- P3 (client → server): the client only needs to acknowledge the server's SYN, so SYN=0, ACK=1 (not SYN=1,ACK=1 as one distractor suggests).

So the correct flags are P1: SYN=1, and P2: SYN=1 & ACK=1.

Answer: P2 (SYN=1, ACK=1), and P1 (SYN=1)

questions.question:
Identify the ONE CORRECT matching between the OSI layers and their corresponding functionalities as shown.
[latex]\begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline \textbf{OSI Layers} & \textbf{Functionalities} \\ \hline \text{(a) Network layer} & \text{(I) Packet routing} \\ \hline \text{(b) Transport layer} & \text{(II) Framing and error handling} \\ \hline \text{(c) Datalink layer} & \text{(III) Host to host communication} \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]
questions.explanation:
Matching OSI layers to their core job:

- Transport layer provides (III) host-to-host communication (end-to-end delivery between the actual communicating processes/hosts).
- Data link layer handles (II) framing and error handling (organizing bits into frames and detecting/correcting transmission errors on a single link).

Answer: (a)-(I), (b)-(III), (c)-(II)

questions.question: Suppose that in an IP-over-Ethernet network, a machine X wishes to find the MAC address of another machine Y in its subnet. Which one of the following techniques can be used for this?

options.A: X sends an ARP request packet to the local gateway's IP address which then finds the  MAC address of Y and sends to X
options.B: X sends an ARP request packet to the local gateway's MAC address which then finds the MAC address of Y and sends to X
options.C: X sends an ARP request packet with broadcast MAC address in its local subnet
options.D: X sends an ARP request packet with broadcast IP address in its local subnet

questions.explanation:
ARP request: X does not know Y's MAC, so it sends the request to the broadcast MAC address (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) in its subnet, carrying Y's IP. Only Y replies, with its MAC.

The gateway is not involved (Y is in the same subnet), and ARP does not use a broadcast IP address.

Answer: X sends an ARP request packet with broadcast MAC address in its local subnet

questions.question: Consider the transmission of data bits [latex]110001011[/latex] over a link that uses Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) code for error detection. If the generator bit pattern is given to be [latex]1001[/latex], which one of the following options shows the remainder bit pattern appended to the data bits before transmission?
questions.explanation:
Perform binary (modulo-2) division of the data (with [latex]3[/latex] zero bits appended, since the generator [latex]1001[/latex] has degree [latex]3[/latex]) by the generator [latex]1001[/latex], where each subtraction step is simply an XOR:

Dividend: [latex]110001011000[/latex] (original data [latex]110001011[/latex] followed by [latex]000[/latex]).
Repeatedly XOR-ing the generator [latex]1001[/latex] into the leading bits wherever the current leading bit is [latex]1[/latex], and shifting along, the division terminates with remainder [latex]100[/latex].

This remainder [latex]100[/latex] is what gets appended to the original data bits to form the transmitted CRC codeword.

Answer: 100

questions.question: Consider the implementation of sliding window protocol over a lossless link, with a window size of [latex]W[/latex] frames, where each frame is of size [latex]1000[/latex] bits (including header). The bandwidth of the link is [latex]100 {kbps}\left(1 {k}=10^{3}\right)[/latex] and the one-way propagation delay is [latex]100[/latex] milliseconds. Assume that processing times at the sender and receiver are zero and the transmission time of acknowledgements is also zero. Which one of the following options gives the minimum size of [latex]W[/latex] (in number of frames) required to achieve [latex]100\%[/latex] link utilization?
questions.explanation:
Transmission time [latex]T_t=\dfrac{\text{frame size}}{\text{bandwidth}}=\dfrac{1000\text{ bits}}{100\times10^3\text{ bps}}=10[/latex] ms.

For [latex]100\%[/latex] link utilization with a sliding window, the sender must be able to keep transmitting continuously until the acknowledgement of the very first frame returns, which takes [latex]T_t+2T_p[/latex] (one-way propagation to receiver, plus one-way for the ack to come back, plus zero processing/ack-transmission time).

So we need: [latex]W\cdot T_t\ge T_t+2T_p\;\Rightarrow\;W\ge1+\dfrac{2T_p}{T_t}=1+\dfrac{2\times100}{10}=1+20=21[/latex].

Answer: 21

questions.question:
Consider the sliding window flow-control protocol operating between a sender and a receiver over a full-duplex error-free link. Assume the following:

The time taken for processing the data frame by the receiver is negligible.
The time taken for processing the acknowledgement frame by the sender is negligible.
The sender has infinite number of frames available for transmission.
The size of the data frame is 2,000 bits and the size of the acknowledgement frame is 10 bits.
The link data rate in each direction is 1 Mbps ([latex]= 10^6[/latex] bits per second).
One way propagation delay of the link is 100 milliseconds.

The minimum value of the sender's window size in terms of the number of frames, (rounded to the nearest integer) needed to achieve a link utilization of 50% is _____________
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Frame transmission time = 2000 / [latex]10^6[/latex] = 2 ms
- ACK transmission time = 10 / [latex]10^6[/latex] = 0.01 ms
- Cycle = 2 + 100 + 0.01 + 100 = 202.01 ms

Utilization [latex]=\frac{W\times2}{202.01}=0.5\Rightarrow W=50.5[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] about 51 frames.

Answer: 51

questions.question:
Consider a network with three routers P, Q, R shown in the figure below. All the links have cost of unity.

The routers exchange distance vector routing information and have converged on the routing tables, after which the link Q-R fails. Assume that P and Q send out routing updates at random times, each at the same average rate. The probability of a routing loop formation (rounded off to one decimal place) between P and Q, leading to count-to-infinity problem, is ____
questions.explanation:
Before failure: Q reaches R at cost 1, P reaches R at cost 2 (via Q). After Q-R fails:
- If Q sends its update first (R unreachable), P learns R is unreachable [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] no loop.
- If P sends first, it still advertises "R at cost 2". Q then sets its route to R via P (cost 3), and P routes through Q [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] routing loop and count-to-infinity.

Both are equally likely, so probability [latex]=0.5[/latex].

Answer: 0.5

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question: Let the size of congestion window of a TCP connection be 32 KB when a timeout occurs. The round trip time of the connection is 100 msec and the maximum segment size used is 2kB. The time taken (in msec) by the TCP connection to get back to 32KB congestion window is ______
questions.explanation:
After the timeout: ssthresh = 16 KB, cwnd = 2 KB (1 MSS).
- Slow start: 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 8 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 16 KB (3 RTTs)
- Congestion avoidance, +2 KB per RTT: 18, 20, [latex]\ldots[/latex], 32 KB (8 RTTs)

Total 11 RTTs [latex]\times[/latex] 100 ms = 1100 ms

Answer: 1100
